authors.name: A. V. Dicey
authors.bio: English jurist of the Vinerian chair at Oxford, expositor of the rule of law and of parliamentary sovereignty. Law and Public Opinion in England of 1905 read a century of legislation as the turning tide between Benthamite individualism and collectivism.

works.evidence: Delivered as Lowell Lectures at Harvard in 1898; first published by Macmillan, London, 1905.

authors.name: Abbé de Mably
authors.bio: French political writer of Grenoble, elder brother of the philosopher Condillac. His four letters to John Adams of 1784 examined the new American state constitutions and pressed republican austerity against the pull of commercial wealth.

works.evidence: Observations sur le gouvernement et les lois des États-Unis d'Amérique, four letters addressed to John Adams, published 1784; English translation issued in London the same year.

authors.notes: Born Gabriel Bonnot de Mably.

authors.name: Abel J. Jones
authors.bio: Welsh educationist and inspector of schools who took a Jena doctorate under Rudolf Eucken himself. His short study of 1912 carried Eucken's activist idealism to English readers in the People's Books series.

works.evidence: First published 1912 by T.C. & E.C. Jack in The People's Books series; Jones's first book.

authors.notes: Dates 1878–1949 from Project Gutenberg and Internet Archive author records; studied under Eucken at Jena, 1905–06.

authors.name: Adam Ferguson
authors.bio: Scottish moral philosopher of the Edinburgh chair, sometime chaplain to the Black Watch regiment. An Essay on the History of Civil Society of 1767 traced the unplanned passage of nations from rudeness to refinement and counted the civic costs of commercial specialization.

authors.name: Adam Smith
authors.bio: Scottish moral philosopher of the Glasgow chair and the Kirkcaldy study. The Wealth of Nations of 1776 organized a century of scattered economic argument into the founding book of political economy.

works.evidence: Student notes of Smith's 1763 Glasgow lectures, first published by Edwin Cannan, Oxford, 1896.

authors.name: Aeschines
authors.bio: Athenian orator, rival of Demosthenes through the long crisis over Philip of Macedon. His three surviving speeches argue the case for peace with Macedon and end in the failed prosecution of the trial of the Crown.

works.evidence: Ancient work (delivered 330 BC); Perseus source, year null per convention.

authors.name: Aeschylus
authors.bio: Athenian tragedian and veteran of Marathon. His seven surviving plays added a second actor to the choral stage and made tragedy an art of dramatic conflict.

works.evidence: Ancient work (produced 458 BC); Perseus source, year null per convention.

authors.name: Albert Moll
authors.bio: Berlin psychiatrist and systematizer of the early science of sexuality, skeptical antagonist of Freud. The Sexual Life of the Child of 1908 placed childhood sexuality under clinical description on lines independent of psychoanalysis.

works.evidence: German original Das Sexualleben des Kindes, Leipzig, 1908; English translation by Eden Paul, 1912.

authors.notes: Of Jewish descent; stripped of his practice under the Nazi regime, he died in Berlin in 1939.

authors.name: Alexander Berkman
authors.bio: Russian-born American anarchist and lifelong companion of Emma Goldman, imprisoned fourteen years for the attempted assassination of the steel magnate Henry Clay Frick. His prison memoir and his primer of communist anarchism are classics of the movement.

authors.name: Alexander Bogdanov
authors.bio: Russian physician, philosopher and Bolshevik, Lenin's rival within the party before the revolution. He built the systems theory he called tektology and wrote on proletarian culture and the philosophy of science.

authors.name: Alexander Philip
authors.bio: Scottish solicitor of Brechin, Fellow of the Royal Society of Edinburgh and campaigner for calendar reform. Essays Towards a Theory of Knowledge of 1915 set out a lawyer's idealist account of perception, causation, and the measurement of time.

works.evidence: First published 1915; the Project Gutenberg text reproduces the Kegan Paul, Trench, Trübner edition of that year.

authors.notes: Death year disputed: Wikipedia and Royal Society of Edinburgh records give 21 January 1932, while the Project Gutenberg author catalog gives 1937; 1932 adopted here. Born 22 May 1858 at Portobello, Edinburgh; elected FRSE 1913.

authors.name: Alexandra Kollontai
authors.bio: Bolshevik revolutionary and the first woman in a modern cabinet, commissar for social welfare after October. She led the Workers' Opposition and wrote on the family, sexuality and the emancipation of women under socialism.

authors.name: Alexis de Tocqueville
authors.bio: Norman aristocrat and magistrate who crossed Jacksonian America to inspect its prisons and stayed to anatomize its democracy. Democracy in America treated equality of conditions as the master fact of the modern age and asked what it would do to liberty.

works.evidence: Volume one 1835, volume two 1840 (already recorded as 1840).
L'Ancien Régime et la Révolution, Paris, 1856; English translation the same year.
Souvenirs, written 1850–51, published posthumously in Paris, 1893; English translation 1896.

authors.name: Alfred Marshall
authors.bio: English economist of the Cambridge chair, teacher of Pigou and Keynes. Principles of Economics of 1890 joined marginal utility to classical cost in the supply-and-demand apparatus that organized the discipline for two generations.

works.evidence: First edition, Macmillan, London, 1890; eighth and final edition 1920.

authors.name: Allama Iqbal
authors.bio: Prominent 20th-century poet, philosopher, and politician widely regarded as having inspired the Pakistan Movement. His poetry in Urdu and Persian explores themes of spiritual renewal, Islamic philosophy, and the empowerment of the individual.

authors.name: American Anti-Slavery Society
authors.bio: Abolitionist organization founded at Philadelphia under William Lloyd Garrison and the Tappan brothers. Its tracts, traveling agents, and petition drives pressed the demand for immediate emancipation on the free states until ratification of the Fifteenth Amendment closed its work.

works.evidence: First series of twenty numbered tracts issued by the Society in New York, 1855–56; 1855 used for the series start.

authors.notes: Organization, not a person, so birth and death fields are null: founded December 1833 in Philadelphia, dissolved 1870 after ratification of the Fifteenth Amendment.

authors.name: Ammianus Marcellinus
authors.bio: Greek-born Roman soldier and historian from Antioch, an officer under the emperor Julian. The Res Gestae took up Roman history where Tacitus left off and is the last major surviving Latin narrative of the empire.

works.evidence: Ancient work (Perseus source); composed c. 380s-390s AD.

authors.notes: Dates conventional approximations: born c. 330 in Antioch, died c. 391-400 (after 391, when the Res Gestae breaks off references). Wrote in Latin though a native Greek speaker.

authors.name: Anatoly Lunacharsky
authors.bio: Bolshevik writer and orator, the Soviet government's first commissar of enlightenment. He shaped early Soviet education and the arts and wrote criticism, drama and essays on religion and culture.

authors.name: Andocides
authors.bio: Athenian orator of the Peloponnesian War generation, implicated in the mutilation of the Herms. His surviving speeches, above all On the Mysteries, are firsthand pleadings from the religious and political scandals of late fifth-century Athens.

works.evidence: Ancient work (Perseus source); transmitted under Andocides' name but generally judged spurious.

authors.notes: Dates approximate: born c. 440 BC, died c. 390 BC (after exile following the speech On the Peace). One of the canonical ten Attic orators. Against Alcibiades is widely considered a later composition.

authors.name: Andrew Dickson White
authors.bio: American historian and diplomat, co-founder and first president of Cornell University. Fiat Money Inflation in France retold the assignat collapse of the 1790s as a warning against the paper-money agitation of postbellum America.

works.evidence: First published 1876 as 'Paper-Money Inflation in France', from a paper read to members of Congress during the greenback controversy; expanded under the present title in 1896 and again in 1912.

authors.notes: Also U.S. minister to Germany and Russia and author of A History of the Warfare of Science with Theology (1896).

authors.name: Andrew Fletcher of Saltoun
authors.bio: Scottish laird, soldier, and member of the last Scottish Parliament, the leading opponent of the parliamentary Union with England. His discourses on militias, trade, and government argued for a self-governing Scotland within a confederated Britain.

works.evidence: Posthumous compilation edited by David Daiches (Scottish Academic Press, 1979); the constituent pamphlets and speeches first appeared 1697-1704.

authors.notes: Year given is for the modern compilation since the work as listed is the Daiches selection, not any single original pamphlet.

authors.name: Anne Robert Jacques Turgot
authors.bio: French economist and administrator, intendant of Limoges and reforming finance minister to Louis XVI. The Reflections set out a theory of capital, saving, and the net product that carried physiocratic economics toward Adam Smith.

works.evidence: Written 1766; first published serially in the Ephemerides du citoyen 1769-70, with a separate printing in 1770.

authors.name: Anselm of Canterbury
authors.bio: Benedictine monk and prior of Bec who became archbishop of Canterbury, born at Aosta in the Alps. The Proslogion's ontological argument and Cur Deus Homo's account of the atonement set the program for scholastic theology.

works.evidence: Medieval treatises (Monologion 1076, Proslogion 1077-78, Cur Deus Homo 1094-98); this combined English volume is Sidney Norton Deane's translation published by Open Court in 1903.

authors.notes: Nationality by birthplace (Aosta, then in the Kingdom of Burgundy, conventionally labeled Italian); career spent in Normandy and England.

authors.name: Antiphon
authors.bio: Athenian orator and speechwriter from Rhamnus, an architect of the oligarchic coup of the Four Hundred. His courtroom speeches and model Tetralogies are the earliest surviving specimens of Attic forensic oratory.
authors.notes: Birth year c. 480 BC approximate; executed 411 BC after the fall of the Four Hundred. Identity question (orator vs. sophist) exists in scholarship but the orator of Rhamnus is the standard attribution for these speeches.

authors.name: Antoine Louis Claude Destutt de Tracy
authors.bio: French philosopher, soldier, and senator who coined the term 'ideology' for his projected science of ideas. His commentary on Montesquieu and his treatise on political economy reached American readers in translations sponsored by Thomas Jefferson.

works.evidence: First published anonymously in English translation at Philadelphia in 1811, arranged by Jefferson; the French text appeared only later (1819).
Original French text published 1815 as the economic part of the Elements d'ideologie (Traite de la volonte); the Jefferson-revised English translation appeared at Georgetown in 1817.

authors.name: Anton Pannekoek
authors.bio: Dutch astronomer and Marxist theorist, a founding voice of council communism in the German and Dutch left. His essays argued that workers' self-organization, not party or trade-union officialdom, is the lever of socialist revolution.

works.evidence: Lecture published as a pamphlet in 1909 (Marxismus und Darwinismus).
Written 1902 as the introduction to Dietzgen's Positive Outcome of Philosophy.
Same 1902 introduction to Dietzgen, duplicate record under a variant title.

authors.notes: Also a professional astronomer of standing (Amsterdam chair; history of astronomy). The two Dietzgen entries are duplicates of one 1902 text.

authors.name: Antonio Gramsci
authors.bio: Sardinian-born journalist and Marxist theorist, founder of L'Ordine Nuovo and head of the Communist Party of Italy until his imprisonment under Mussolini. The factory-council articles collected here worked out a politics of workers' democracy that the later Prison Notebooks generalized into the theory of hegemony.

works.evidence: Article in Avanti!, December 1917, on the Bolshevik revolution.
Report written for the Communist International, 1921.

authors.notes: Died 1937 in Rome shortly after release from Fascist imprisonment on health grounds.

authors.name: Antonio Labriola
authors.bio: Italian philosopher of the Naples chair, the first to give Marxism a rigorous philosophical statement in Italy. His essays on the materialist conception of history treated it as an open method of inquiry rather than a closed system, and shaped the young Gramsci and Croce.

authors.name: Apollodorus
authors.bio: Greek mythographer, conventionally called Pseudo-Apollodorus and long misidentified with the Athenian grammarian Apollodorus of Athens. The Library and its Epitome condense the genealogies and hero-cycles of Greek myth into a single systematic handbook.
authors.notes: Dates null by design: the author is the anonymous 'Pseudo-Apollodorus'; the traditional attribution to Apollodorus of Athens (2nd century BC) is rejected on internal evidence.

authors.name: Appianus of Alexandria
authors.bio: Greek historian from Alexandria who practiced as an advocate at Rome and obtained a procuratorship under Antoninus Pius. His Roman History, arranged war by war and people by people, preserves the fullest surviving narrative of the civil wars that ended the Republic.
authors.notes: Dates conventional approximations: c. AD 95 - c. 165. All listed works are sections of the single Roman History (Rhomaika), written in Greek.

authors.name: Apuleius
authors.bio: Latin prose writer from Madauros in Roman North Africa, trained in rhetoric at Carthage and Athens. The Metamorphoses, the only Latin novel to survive complete, set the tale of Cupid and Psyche inside the story of a man transformed into an ass.

works.evidence: Ancient work (2nd century AD); Perseus source, no publication year per instructions.

authors.notes: Dates approximate: born c. 124 AD, died after c. 170 AD; standard reference convention.

authors.name: Aretaeus of Cappadocia
authors.bio: Greek physician of Cappadocia who wrote in the Ionic dialect in conscious imitation of Hippocrates. His four treatises on acute and chronic diseases gave clinical accounts of diabetes, tetanus, and pleurisy that physicians cited into the nineteenth century.
authors.notes: Floruit author: usually placed in the 1st century AD (some scholars argue 2nd century); birth and death years genuinely unknown, hence null.

authors.name: Aristophanes
authors.bio: Athenian comic playwright of Old Comedy during the Peloponnesian War. His surviving plays turned Athenian politics and intellectual life into stage satire, and Clouds preserved the earliest caricature of Socrates.

works.evidence: Ancient comedy (first staged 414 BC); Perseus source.
Ancient comedy (first staged 423 BC); Perseus source.

authors.notes: Dates conventional approximations: c. 446 - c. 386 BC.

authors.name: Aristotle
authors.bio: Philosopher of Stagira, student of Plato and tutor of Alexander. His school texts organized the sciences for two millennia and traveled further than any other body of work in this library's atlas.

authors.name: Arthur Cecil Pigou
authors.bio: English economist who succeeded Alfred Marshall in the Cambridge chair of political economy. The Economics of Welfare of 1920 worked out the analysis of externalities and the case for corrective taxes that came to carry his name.

works.evidence: First edition published by Macmillan, London, 1920; expanded from Wealth and Welfare (1912).

authors.name: Arthur Young
authors.bio: English agricultural writer and surveyor of farming practice at home and abroad. His Travels in France described the countryside on the eve of the Revolution and became a standard source for its historians.

works.evidence: First edition published at Bury St. Edmunds, 1792; a second, two-volume edition followed in 1794.

authors.name: Athenaeus of Naucratis
authors.bio: Greek grammarian from Naucratis in Egypt, writing under the Severan emperors. The Deipnosophistae, a learned banquet conversation in fifteen books, preserved quotations from hundreds of Greek authors otherwise lost.
authors.notes: Floruit author: active c. late 2nd to early 3rd century AD; birth and death years unknown, hence null.

authors.name: Auberon Herbert and J. H. Levy
authors.bio: English individualists of the Personal Rights Association, Herbert the advocate of voluntaryism and Levy the editor who pressed the case against him. Taxation and Anarchism of 1912 printed their exchange on whether a state could be financed without compulsion.

works.evidence: Published by the Personal Rights Association, London, 1912, after Herbert's death in 1906 (OLL title record).

authors.notes: Composite author record, so birth/death null. Individually: Auberon Herbert 1838-1906, Joseph Hiam Levy 1838-1913.

authors.name: August Bebel
authors.bio: Saxon master turner who co-founded German Social Democracy with Wilhelm Liebknecht and led the party for four decades. Woman and Socialism of 1879 tied the emancipation of women to the socialist program and ran through more than fifty editions in his lifetime.

works.evidence: Existing year retained; speech/article from 1905 per Marxists Internet Archive.
Existing year retained; 1899 per Marxists Internet Archive.

authors.name: Augustin Thierry
authors.bio: French historian of the Romantic school, early secretary to Saint-Simon and blind through his later working years. The Recits des temps merovingiens of 1840 turned the chronicles of Frankish Gaul into narrative history built on primary sources.

works.evidence: English compilation first published 1845 (Philadelphia: Carey and Hart), combining Dix ans d'etudes historiques (1835) and Recits des temps merovingiens (1840).

authors.name: Augustine of Hippo
authors.bio: Bishop of Hippo in Roman North Africa, a convert to Christianity under Ambrose of Milan. The Confessions and the City of God fixed the Western Christian understanding of sin, grace, and history for a thousand years.

works.evidence: Ancient correspondence (late 4th-early 5th century AD); Perseus source.

authors.notes: Born at Thagaste in Roman Numidia; 'Roman' used as the conventional label.

authors.name: Ausonius, Decimus Magnus
authors.bio: Gallo-Roman poet and professor of rhetoric at Bordeaux, tutor to the future emperor Gratian and consul in 379. His epigrams, verse letters, and formal thanksgiving for the consulship recorded the literary culture of fourth-century Gaul.

works.evidence: Speech of thanks for the consulship of 379 AD; Perseus source.

authors.notes: Dates approximate: c. 310 - c. 395 AD; standard reference convention.

authors.name: Averroes (Ibn Rushd)
authors.bio: Cordoban judge, physician, and commentator on Aristotle under the Almohad caliphs. His commentaries carried Aristotle back into Latin Europe and set off the scholastic quarrel over reason and revelation.

works.evidence: English translation by Mohammad Jamil-ur-Rehman published at Baroda, 1921 (Gaekwad Studies in Religion and Philosophy XI); underlying Arabic treatises composed in the 12th century.

authors.notes: Born in Cordoba, died in Marrakesh; 'Andalusian' used as the conventional label.

authors.name: Bacchylides
authors.bio: Greek lyric poet from the island of Ceos, nephew of Simonides and rival of Pindar for the same patrons. His victory odes and dithyrambs, recovered from an Egyptian papyrus in the late nineteenth century, form the largest surviving body of Greek choral lyric after Pindar.

works.evidence: Ancient work transmitted via papyrus; Perseus source, so published_year null per instructions.
Ancient work transmitted via papyrus; Perseus source, so published_year null per instructions.

authors.name: Barnabae Epistula
authors.bio: Anonymous Greek-writing Christian of the generation after the apostles, traditionally and mistakenly credited as Paul's companion Barnabas. The epistle reads the Jewish scriptures as allegory and claims their covenant for the church rather than the synagogue.

works.evidence: Ancient work (composed c. 70-132 AD); Perseus source, so published_year null per instructions.

authors.notes: Pseudonymous/anonymous author; modern scholarship rejects the attribution to the apostolic Barnabas, hence null dates and nationality. Composition usually placed between c. 70 and 132 AD, possibly in Alexandria.

authors.name: Baron d'Holbach
authors.bio: German-born French philosophe whose Paris salon fed and sheltered the Encyclopedists. His tracts, printed abroad under borrowed names to escape the censor, attacked revealed religion and defended atheism outright.

works.evidence: Histoire critique de Jesus-Christ published clandestinely c. 1770 (year as given; standard dating).

authors.name: Baruch Spinoza
authors.bio: Amsterdam-born philosopher of Portuguese-Jewish descent, expelled from his congregation and supported afterward by grinding lenses. The Ethics set out a God identical with nature in geometrical proofs, and the Theologico-Political Treatise opened the modern case for freedom of thought.

works.evidence: Ethica published posthumously in the Opera Posthuma, 1677.

authors.name: Bede
authors.bio: Northumbrian monk of the twin monastery of Wearmouth-Jarrow, scholar of scripture, chronology, and history. The Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation gave the English their first connected history and spread the dating of years from the Incarnation.

works.evidence: Medieval work (completed 731); Perseus source, so published_year null per instructions.

authors.notes: Birth year conventionally given as 672/673; 673 used here. Died 26 May 735. 'English' used as the conventional label for Anglo-Saxon Northumbria.

authors.name: Benedetto Croce
authors.bio: Neapolitan philosopher and historian, editor of the journal La Critica and a senator who became liberal Italy's chief intellectual opponent of Fascism. His early essays on historical materialism examined and rejected Marx's economics, the first step toward his own idealist system of aesthetics and historiography.

works.evidence: Year as given: 1914 is the first English edition (trans. C. M. Meredith); the Italian Materialismo storico ed economia marxistica collected essays of 1896-1899 and appeared in 1900.

authors.name: Benjamin Constant
authors.bio: Swiss-born French political writer, novelist, and liberal deputy under the Restoration. His lecture on ancient and modern liberty separated the freedom to participate in politics from the freedom to live unmolested, a distinction that became standard in liberal thought.

works.evidence: Delivered as a lecture at the Athenee Royal in Paris in February 1819 and published that year.

authors.notes: Born in Lausanne to a family of Huguenot descent; his political career and writing were French, so French is the conventional label (sometimes given as Swiss-French).

authors.name: Bertrand Russell
authors.bio: British logician and philosopher, co-author with Whitehead of Principia Mathematica and a public dissenter through two world wars. His shorter books carried the analytic method into epistemology, psychology, and politics for a general readership.

works.evidence: Mysticism and Logic and Other Essays first published by Longmans, Green in 1918.
Our Knowledge of the External World, the 1914 Lowell Lectures, published by Open Court in 1914.
Political Ideals first published by The Century Co., New York, 1917.
Roads to Freedom published in London 1918 (American edition as Proposed Roads to Freedom, 1919); original publication 1918.
The Analysis of Mind first published by Allen and Unwin in 1921.

authors.name: Blaise Pascal
authors.bio: French mathematician and physicist drawn into the Jansenist circle of Port-Royal after a religious conversion. The Pensees, fragments of an unfinished defense of Christianity published after his death, argue from the misery and greatness of man to the necessity of faith.

works.evidence: Pensees first published posthumously in the Port-Royal edition of 1670.

authors.notes: The source era label 'Renaissance' is loose; Pascal belongs to the seventeenth century.

authors.name: Boethius
authors.bio: Roman senator and consul under the Ostrogothic king Theoderic, translator of Aristotle's logic into Latin. The Consolation of Philosophy, written in prison while he awaited execution, carried Platonic argument about fortune and providence through the Latin Middle Ages.

authors.name: Bruce Smith
authors.bio: Australian barrister and free-trade politician, organizer of employers' associations and a parliamentary opponent of the White Australia policy. Liberty and Liberalism argued the classical liberal case against protection and the expanding colonial state.

works.evidence: Liberty and Liberalism published in Melbourne in 1887 (confirmed via Wikipedia, the Australian Dictionary of Biography, and OLL).

authors.notes: Full name Arthur Bruce Smith KC (28 June 1851 - 14 August 1937); born in Glasgow, career entirely in the Australian colonies and federal parliament, so Australian is the conventional label. Verified by web search.

authors.name: Carl L. Becker
authors.bio: American historian of the Cornell faculty, trained under Frederick Jackson Turner and a skeptic about the certainty of historical knowledge. His study of the Declaration of Independence traced the document's drafting and its natural-rights philosophy to their eighteenth-century sources.

works.evidence: The Declaration of Independence: A Study in the History of Political Ideas first published by Harcourt, Brace in 1922.

authors.notes: Carl Lotus Becker, 1873-1945; professor at Cornell from 1917.

authors.name: Carl Menger
authors.bio: Austrian economist, founder of the Vienna school and tutor in economics to Crown Prince Rudolf. The Grundsätze der Volkswirtschaftslehre of 1871 derived value from marginal utility and opened the Methodenstreit with the German historical school.

works.evidence: First published Vienna: Wilhelm Braumüller, 1871; founding text of Austrian marginal utility theory.

authors.name: Carl von Clausewitz
authors.bio: Prussian general and military theorist who served through the Napoleonic wars. His unfinished On War, with its account of war as the continuation of policy by other means, became the most influential study of its subject.

authors.name: Carveth Read
authors.bio: English philosopher and logician, professor of philosophy of mind and logic at University College London. Logic: Deductive and Inductive of 1898 supplied a plain-language textbook that ran through four editions and decades of classroom use.

works.evidence: First edition London: Grant Richards, 1898; the Project Gutenberg text is a later revised edition of the same work.

authors.name: Catharine Macaulay
authors.bio: English republican historian, author of an eight-volume History of England read on both sides of the Atlantic revolutions. Her Observations of 1790 answered Burke's Reflections within weeks and defended the French Revolution on Whig principles.

works.evidence: Published London 1790, among the earliest replies to Burke's Reflections on the Revolution in France (1790).

authors.name: Catullus, C. Valerius
authors.bio: Roman poet from Verona, central figure of the late-Republican circle of 'new poets.' His carmina carried Greek lyric and epigram into Latin and fixed the vocabulary of personal poetry around the affair with Lesbia.

works.evidence: Ancient poetry collection transmitted by manuscript; Perseus source, no publication year.

authors.notes: Dates c. 84–c. 54 BC are the conventional approximations derived from Jerome, adjusted by modern scholarship.

authors.name: Celsus, Aulus Cornelius
authors.bio: Roman encyclopaedist of the early Empire, compiler of the Artes covering agriculture, rhetoric, warfare, and medicine. De Medicina, the one surviving section, preserved the fullest ancient account of Hellenistic and Roman medical practice.

works.evidence: Ancient treatise composed under Tiberius; Perseus source, no publication year.

authors.notes: Floruit author: active under Tiberius, c. AD 25–35. The conventional dates c. 25 BC–c. AD 50 are conjectural, so birth and death years are left null.

authors.name: Cesare Beccaria
authors.bio: Milanese marquis and jurist of the circle around the Verri brothers and their journal Il Caffè. Dei delitti e delle pene of 1764 argued against torture and the death penalty and set the program of Enlightenment penal reform.

works.evidence: Dei delitti e delle pene first published anonymously at Livorno, 1764; the standard English translation appeared in 1767.

authors.notes: Year given is the original Italian publication; the OLL English text derives from the 1767 translation.

authors.name: Charles Comte
authors.bio: French lawyer and journalist, co-founder with Charles Dunoyer of Le Censeur and son-in-law of Jean-Baptiste Say. The Traité de législation of 1827 explained the prosperity of peoples by their industrious habits rather than their laws, and armed a generation of French liberals.

authors.name: Charles Darwin
authors.bio: English naturalist of the Beagle voyage and the Down House study. On the Origin of Species of 1859 established evolution by natural selection as the organizing principle of the life sciences.

works.evidence: First published London: John Murray, 24 November 1859.

authors.name: Charles Dunoyer
authors.bio: French economist and journalist, co-editor with Charles Comte of Le Censeur under the Restoration. The Nouveau traité d'économie sociale of 1830 recast political economy as the study of free human industry displacing the rule of the warrior class.

works.evidence: First published Paris: Sautelet et Mesnier, 2 volumes, 1830 (BnF/Gallica catalog); a reworking of his 1825 L'Industrie et la morale.
First published Paris: Sautelet et Mesnier, 2 volumes, 1830 (BnF/Gallica catalog).

authors.name: Charles Francis Bastable
authors.bio: Irish economist, holder of the Whately chair of political economy at Trinity College Dublin for half a century. Public Finance of 1892 gave English-language economics its first systematic treatise on taxation and public expenditure.

works.evidence: First edition London: Macmillan, 1892; revised editions followed in 1895 and 1903.

authors.name: Charles Wentworth Dilke
authors.bio: English critic and antiquary, editor of the Athenaeum and friend of Keats. The anonymous 1821 pamphlet on the source of national difficulties drew a critique of capital from Ricardian premises and was later singled out by Marx.

works.evidence: Published anonymously, London 1821 (year supplied in source data); attribution to Dilke is the standard scholarly one.

authors.notes: This is C. W. Dilke the elder (1789–1864), grandfather of the politician. The pamphlet appeared anonymously; its attribution to Dilke is conventional in Marx scholarship but not contemporaneously documented.

authors.name: Cicero (Marcus Tullius Cicero)
authors.bio: Roman orator and consul, defender of the Republic against Catiline and Antony. His speeches, treatises, and letters carried Greek philosophy into Latin and fixed the prose style of Europe for centuries.

works.evidence: Ancient correspondence collected and circulated posthumously in antiquity; null per ancient-work rule. The OLL edition is Evelyn Shuckburgh's English translation (1899–1900).

authors.notes: Ancient work via OLL: original 'publication' is antiquity, so the year is null; the OLL text is a modern translation.

authors.name: Cicero, Marcus Tullius
authors.bio: Roman orator and statesman of the late Republic, consul in the year of the Catilinarian conspiracy. His courtroom and senate speeches set the standard of Latin prose, and his late treatises gave Rome a Latin vocabulary for Greek philosophy.
authors.notes: 106-43 BC; murdered in the proscriptions of the Second Triumvirate, December 43 BC. All listed works are ancient Perseus texts, so published_year is null throughout. Catalog era label 'Hellenistic' is loose; he is a Roman Republican author.

authors.name: Clara Zetkin
authors.bio: German socialist organizer, editor of Die Gleichheit and founder of International Women's Day. Her writings tied the workers' movement to women's suffrage and gave the Communist International its first sustained analysis of fascism.
authors.notes: Born Wiederau, Saxony, 1857; died in exile near Moscow, 1933. Existing work years verified: Fascism (Labour Monthly, 1923), report to the Third Enlarged ECCI Plenum (June 1923), suffrage speech (1906), women's movement article (1909), Through Dictatorship to Democracy (1919).

works.evidence: Article of 1909 on the German socialist women's movement.
Speech at the Mannheim socialist women's conference, 1906.
Report to the Third Enlarged Plenum of the ECCI, June 1923.

authors.name: Claudian
authors.bio: Alexandrian-born Latin poet at the court of the emperor Honorius and his general Stilicho. His panegyrics and invectives turned the politics of the divided empire into epic verse, the last sustained poetry in the classical Latin manner.
authors.notes: Claudius Claudianus, conventionally c. 370 - c. 404 AD: birth year is an estimate and he disappears from the record after 404, presumed dead soon after. Greek-speaking Alexandrian by origin who wrote in Latin; labeled Roman by convention. All works ancient (Perseus), publication years not applicable.

authors.name: Clemens Romanus (Clement of Rome)
authors.bio: Bishop of Rome at the close of the first century, counted among the Apostolic Fathers. The letter to the Corinthians sent under his name is the earliest datable Christian writing outside the New Testament; the second epistle bearing his name is an anonymous sermon of a later generation.
authors.notes: Fl. c. 96 AD, when 1 Clement was written. The traditional death date of c. 99 and the martyrdom account rest on later legend, so both years are left null. 2 Clement is universally regarded as not his work but a mid-2nd-century homily transmitted under his name. Perseus texts, so publication years not applicable.

authors.name: Columella, Lucius Junius Moderatus
authors.bio: Roman writer on agriculture from Gades in Spain, an army tribune turned farmer of Italian estates. The twelve books of his Res Rustica are the fullest account of farming to survive from the ancient world.
authors.notes: Born Gades (modern Cadiz) c. 4 AD; died c. 70 AD. Both years are conventional approximations from standard references. Perseus text, publication year not applicable.

authors.name: Condy Raguet
authors.bio: Philadelphia merchant and economist who served as the first United States charge d'affaires to Brazil. The Principles of Free Trade gathered his Banner of the Constitution essays into an early American brief against the protective tariff.
authors.notes: Born Philadelphia, January 28, 1784; died March 1842. Pennsylvania state senator, free-trade journal editor (The Free Trade Advocate, The Banner of the Constitution), and US charge d'affaires to Brazil 1825-27. Dates and 1835 publication verified via Wikipedia, OLL, and HathiTrust catalog records.

works.evidence: The Principles of Free Trade, Illustrated in a Series of Short and Familiar Essays, Philadelphia, 1835; compiled from his Banner of the Constitution articles (2nd ed. 1840).

authors.name: Constantin-François Volney
authors.bio: French orientalist and traveler in Egypt and Syria, deputy to the Estates-General of 1789. The Ruins of 1791 read the fall of empires as an argument for natural law and religious skepticism, and became a standard text of revolutionary-era freethought.
authors.notes: Constantin-Francois Chasseboeuf, comte de Volney, 1757-1820. Imprisoned under the Terror, later senator and count under Napoleon and peer under the Restoration.

works.evidence: Les Ruines, ou meditations sur les revolutions des empires, Paris, 1791; first English translation 1792.

authors.name: Cynewulf
authors.bio: Old English poet known only from the runic signatures woven into four religious poems. Elene and Juliana recast saints' legends in alliterative verse and stand among the few Old English poems with a named author.
authors.notes: Fl. 9th century (scholarship ranges from late 8th to early 10th); nothing biographical is known beyond the runic acrostic signatures, so dates are null. The four signed poems are Juliana, Elene, Christ II, and The Fates of the Apostles; Andreas is anonymous and the older attribution to Cynewulf, reflected in our catalog, is rejected by modern scholarship. Years given for works are the first printed editions of the medieval texts.

works.evidence: Vercelli Book poem first printed in Jacob Grimm, Andreas und Elene, Cassel, 1840. Anonymous; not actually by Cynewulf.
Vercelli Book poem first printed in Jacob Grimm, Andreas und Elene, Cassel, 1840.
Exeter Book poem first printed in Benjamin Thorpe's Codex Exoniensis, London, 1842.

authors.name: Daniel De Leon
authors.bio: Curacao-born editor of the Socialist Labor Party's Daily People and theorist of socialist industrial unionism. His strike addresses and Socialist Reconstruction of Society set out a program of industrial unions taking and holding the means of production.
authors.notes: Born Curacao 1852, emigrated to the US, led the Socialist Labor Party from the 1890s and co-founded the IWW in 1905; died New York 1914. Existing work years verified: Reform or Revolution (address, 1896), What Means This Strike? (address, 1898), The Burning Question of Trades Unionism (address, 1904), Socialist Reconstruction of Society (address, 1905).

works.evidence: Address delivered in New Bedford, February 11, 1898.

authors.name: Dante Alighieri
authors.bio: Florentine poet of the Commedia, exiled in the faction fights of his city. De Monarchia argued in Latin that the universal emperor holds authority directly from God, owing nothing to the papacy.
authors.notes: Born Florence 1265, died Ravenna 1321. De Monarchia was written c. 1312-13, condemned and burned in 1329, and placed on the Index in 1554; first printed edition Basel, 1559.

works.evidence: Latin treatise written c. 1312-13; first printed edition Basel (Oporinus), 1559.

authors.name: David Hume
authors.bio: Scottish philosopher and historian of the Edinburgh Enlightenment, friend and correspondent of Adam Smith. The Treatise and the Enquiries that recast it pressed empiricism to skeptical conclusions about causation and induction that philosophy has been answering ever since.
authors.notes: 1711-1776, Edinburgh. All publication years are standard: Treatise Books I-II 1739 (Book III 1740); first Enquiry 1748; second Enquiry 1751; Natural History of Religion 1757; Dialogues posthumous 1779.

works.evidence: Books I-II published anonymously, London, 1739; Book III followed in 1740.
First published 1748 as Philosophical Essays concerning Human Understanding; retitled 1758.
Posthumous; published 1779 under the supervision of his nephew.

authors.name: David Riazanov
authors.bio: Russian Marx scholar from Odessa, founder and first director of the Marx-Engels Institute in Moscow. His archival editions of Marx and Engels began the project of their complete collected works before his arrest and execution in the Stalin purges.
authors.notes: Born Odessa 1870; expelled from the Party 1931, shot January 1938 during the Great Purge, rehabilitated 1990. Existing work years kept as given: Karl Marx on China (Labour Monthly, 1926) and the three 1928 pieces from English-language Marxist journals.

authors.name: David Ricardo
authors.bio: English political economist of the London stock exchange and a Member of Parliament, the leading systematizer of the classical school after Smith. His Principles of Political Economy and Taxation built the theories of comparative advantage, rent, and labor value that organized economic reasoning for a century.

works.evidence: OLL hosts the McCulloch collected edition; first issued 1846 (reprinted 1888), gathering Ricardo's writings posthumously.

authors.name: David Starr Jordan
authors.bio: American ichthyologist, peace activist, and founding president of Stanford University. The Philosophy of Despair drew on his naturalist's optimism to argue against pessimism and the romanticizing of failure.

works.evidence: First published 1902 by P. Elder and M. Shepard, San Francisco; Internet Archive and reference sources confirm the date.

authors.name: Demades
authors.bio: Athenian orator and politician of the generation of Demosthenes, known for his pro-Macedonian diplomacy after Chaeronea. The single surviving speech attributed to him survives largely as a fragmentary witness to Athenian oratory in the age of Philip and Alexander.

works.evidence: Perseus/ancient text; no modern publication year.

authors.name: Demosthenes
authors.bio: Athenian statesman and the foremost orator of classical Greece, leader of the resistance to Philip of Macedon. His political and forensic speeches became the canonical standard of Attic prose and rhetorical art.

authors.name: Denis Diderot
authors.bio: French Enlightenment philosopher and chief editor of the Encyclopedie, the great collaborative compendium of the age. His essays, dialogues, and fiction carried materialist and skeptical argument into literary form, much of it circulated or published only after his death.

works.evidence: Le Neveu de Rameau written c. 1761-1774 but unpublished in his lifetime; first appeared 1805 in Goethe's German translation.

authors.name: Desiderius Erasmus
authors.bio: Dutch humanist scholar, priest, and the leading classical and biblical philologist of the northern Renaissance. His satires, devotional manuals, and critical edition of the Greek New Testament shaped both humanist learning and the Reformation debates he sought to moderate.

works.evidence: Moriae Encomium first printed 1511 in Paris; standard date.
Enchiridion militis Christiani first published 1503 (in Lucubratiunculae).

authors.name: DeWitt H. Parker
authors.bio: American philosopher and longtime chair of the philosophy department at the University of Michigan. The Principles of Aesthetics offered a systematic account of aesthetic value drawing on psychology and the history of the arts.

works.evidence: First edition published 1920 by Silver, Burdett and Company, Boston; multiple booksellers and Gutenberg confirm.

authors.name: Didache
authors.bio: Anonymous early Christian church manual of the late first or early second century, also titled The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles. The text sets out instruction on the Two Ways, baptism, the Eucharist, and church order for early congregations.
authors.notes: Anonymous compilation; no individual author, hence null dates.

authors.name: Dinarchus
authors.bio: Corinthian-born logographer active in Athens, counted as the last of the ten canonical Attic orators. His surviving speeches, written for the Harpalus prosecutions, are the chief witness to his career as a professional speechwriter.

authors.name: Diogenes Laertius
authors.bio: Greek biographer of the third century, author of a compilation of the lives and doctrines of the ancient philosophers. His Lives of Eminent Philosophers is the principal surviving source for the biographies and teachings of many Greek thinkers whose own works are lost.
authors.notes: Biographical dates unknown; conventionally placed fl. early 3rd century AD, hence null birth/death.

authors.name: Édouard Le Roy
authors.bio: French philosopher and mathematician, a disciple of Henri Bergson who succeeded him at the Collège de France. His A New Philosophy: Henri Bergson presented Bergson's thought to a general readership as an introduction to the new vitalist philosophy.

works.evidence: English translation (trans. Vincent Benson) published 1913; based on articles in Revue des Deux Mondes, 1912.

authors.notes: Original French articles 1912; English-language book first appeared 1913.

authors.name: Eduard Bernstein
authors.bio: German social-democratic theorist and politician, a friend and literary executor of Engels who broke with orthodox Marxism. His writings launched the revisionist current, arguing that socialism could be reached through democratic reform rather than revolutionary collapse.

authors.name: Edward Bellamy
authors.bio: American journalist and novelist of Massachusetts, originator of the Nationalist reform movement. Looking Backward imagined a cooperative socialist America of the year 2000 and became one of the most widely read utopian novels of its century.

authors.name: Edwin Cannan
authors.bio: British economist of the London School of Economics and editor of the standard scholarly edition of Smith's Wealth of Nations. Wealth compressed his LSE lectures into a short primer on the causes of economic welfare for the general reader.

works.evidence: First edition published by P. S. King & Son, London, 1914; later editions 1928, 1930.

authors.notes: Born in Madeira to British parents; professor at LSE 1907-1926. His 1904 edition of the Wealth of Nations remained standard for most of the century.

authors.name: Edwin Chadwick and Nassau William Senior
authors.bio: English sanitary reformer and Oxford political economist, the working pair behind the Royal Commission into the operation of the poor laws. Their report condemned outdoor relief for the able-bodied and supplied the blueprint for the workhouse system of the New Poor Law.

works.evidence: Report of the Royal Commission for Inquiring into the Administration and Practical Operation of the Poor Laws, published 1834, preceding the Poor Law Amendment Act of that year.

authors.notes: Joint record: birth/death fields left null because two people are covered. Chadwick 1800-1890 (assistant commissioner, later secretary of the Poor Law Commission); Senior 1790-1864 (first Drummond Professor of Political Economy at Oxford). Both English.

authors.name: Eli F. Heckscher
authors.bio: Swedish economic historian of the Stockholm School of Economics, co-originator of the factor-proportions theory of trade later named for him and Ohlin. The Continental System read Napoleon's blockade of Britain as a sustained experiment in economic warfare and judged it a failure.

works.evidence: Swedish original Kontinentalsystemet published 1918; English translation The Continental System: An Economic Interpretation issued by Oxford/Clarendon for the Carnegie Endowment in 1922.

authors.notes: Also author of the two-volume Mercantilism (1931). The OLL edition is the 1922 English translation.

authors.name: Émile Faguet
authors.bio: French literary critic and historian of ideas, professor at the Sorbonne and member of the Académie française. His Initiation into Philosophy offered a compact survey of the history of Western thought for the general reader.

works.evidence: English translation (trans. Sir Homer Gordon) published 1914; from the French initiation series of the period.

authors.notes: English translation date 1914 confirmed via Gutenberg/Internet Archive; exact French original date of this specific title not pinned down, so medium confidence on the year.

authors.name: Emma Goldman
authors.bio: Russian-born American anarchist and agitator, editor of the journal Mother Earth and a tireless lecturer for free speech and birth control. Deported to Soviet Russia after the First World War, she became an early anarchist critic of the Bolshevik state.

authors.name: Epictetus
authors.bio: Greek Stoic philosopher, born a slave in Phrygia, who taught in Rome until Domitian's expulsion of the philosophers and then at Nicopolis. The Discourses and Handbook, taken down by his student Arrian, turned Stoicism into a practical discipline of distinguishing what is in our power from what is not.

works.evidence: Ancient work (Perseus); recorded by Arrian c. AD 108.
Ancient work (Perseus); Arrian's epitome of the Discourses (Enchiridion).
Ancient text in translation (OLL collected edition of the Discourses, Enchiridion, and Fragments); original is ancient, so no publication year.

authors.notes: Conventional dates c. AD 50 - c. 135, both approximate. Wrote nothing himself; all surviving works are Arrian's transcriptions.

authors.name: Ernest Belfort Bax
authors.bio: English socialist philosopher and journalist, a founder of the Social Democratic Federation and collaborator of William Morris. He sought to give Marxism an ethical and metaphysical grounding and wrote widely on history and the philosophy of right.

authors.name: Errico Malatesta
authors.bio: Italian anarchist agitator and propagandist, for half a century the most influential figure in the Italian movement. His writings argued for an anarchist communism reached through insurrection and free association, against both parliamentary socialism and individualist anarchism.

authors.name: Étienne de La Boétie
authors.bio: French magistrate, humanist, and close friend of Montaigne, who memorialized him in the Essays. The Discourse of Voluntary Servitude asked why people consent to tyranny and located the answer in habit and self-subjection rather than force.

works.evidence: Written c. 1548-1553; first printed posthumously in 1576 (in Reveille-Matin des Francais), full text 1577.

authors.notes: Born 1530, died 1563. Discourse written in youth but circulated/printed posthumously; 1576 is the conventional first-print date.

authors.name: Euclid
authors.bio: Greek mathematician of Alexandria, compiler of the Elements under the early Ptolemies. The Elements arranged the geometry of his predecessors into a single deductive system and remained the standard textbook of the subject for over two thousand years.

works.evidence: Ancient work (Perseus), composed c. 300 BC; per registry rules ancient works carry no publication year.

authors.notes: fl. c. 300 BC in Alexandria; birth and death years genuinely unknown, hence null. Almost nothing is known of his life beyond his city and his book.

authors.name: Eugen Richter
authors.bio: German left-liberal politician, leader of the Free-minded opposition to Bismarck in the Reichstag. Pictures of the Socialistic Future narrated the collapse of a socialist Germany through a worker's family diary, a satire aimed at the program of the Social Democrats.

works.evidence: German original Sozialdemokratische Zukunftsbilder published 1891; English translation Pictures of the Socialistic Future appeared 1893.

authors.notes: Longtime editor of the Freisinnige Zeitung; opposed both Bismarck's state socialism and the SPD.

authors.name: Eugen Varga
authors.bio: Hungarian economist, commissar of the 1919 Soviet Republic in Budapest and afterward the Comintern's chief economic analyst in Moscow. His surveys of the postwar capitalist economies set the official Communist reading of crises, reparations, and the prospects of revolution.

works.evidence: Year supplied by the Marxists Internet Archive source record.

authors.notes: Later director of the Institute of World Economy and World Politics in Moscow (1927-1947); his 1946 book on postwar capitalism brought official censure under Stalin.

authors.name: Eugen von Böhm-Bawerk
authors.bio: Austrian economist of the Vienna school and three times finance minister of the Habsburg monarchy. Capital and Interest and The Positive Theory of Capital grounded the Austrian account of interest in time preference and roundabout production, and his critique of Marx's third volume became the standard non-Marxist rejoinder.

works.evidence: Geschichte und Kritik der Kapitalzins-Theorien, vol. 1 of Kapital und Kapitalzins, published 1884; William Smart's English translation 1890.
Positive Theorie des Kapitales, vol. 2 of Kapital und Kapitalzins, published 1889; Smart's English translation 1891.

authors.notes: Brother-in-law and colleague of Friedrich von Wieser; teacher of Mises and Schumpeter in his Vienna seminar.

authors.name: Euripides
authors.bio: Athenian tragedian, youngest of the three great masters of the form and a contemporary of the sophists. His plays brought ordinary speech and disordered passion onto the tragic stage, and more of them survive than of Aeschylus and Sophocles combined.

works.evidence: Ancient work (Perseus); only complete surviving satyr play.
Ancient work (Perseus); produced 428 BC, first prize.
Ancient work (Perseus); transmitted under Euripides' name, authorship disputed.

authors.notes: Conventional dates c. 480 - 406 BC; birth year approximate. Died in Macedonia at the court of Archelaus. Rhesus is included in the corpus though its authorship is debated.

authors.name: Evgeni Preobrazhensky
authors.bio: Bolshevik economist of the Left Opposition and co-author of the ABC of Communism. His theory of primitive socialist accumulation framed the Soviet industrialization debate before he was expelled from the party and shot.

authors.name: Ferdinand Lassalle
authors.bio: German socialist agitator and founder of the General German Workers' Association, the first independent workers' party in Germany. His campaign for state-aided cooperatives and universal suffrage shaped early German social democracy and drew Marx's sustained polemical fire.

authors.name: Flavius Josephus
authors.bio: Jewish priest and rebel commander in Galilee who surrendered to Vespasian and wrote under Flavian patronage in Rome. The Jewish War and the Antiquities preserve the only continuous account of Judaea's revolt against Rome and much of the nation's earlier history.

works.evidence: Ancient work (Perseus); apologetic treatise, c. AD 94-100.
Ancient work (Perseus); autobiographical appendix to the Antiquities.

authors.notes: Born Yosef ben Mattityahu in Jerusalem, AD 37; death c. AD 100, year approximate. Took the Flavian name on receiving Roman citizenship.

authors.name: Francis Amasa Walker
authors.bio: American economist and statistician, Union general, superintendent of two federal censuses, and president of MIT. The Wages Question broke the wages-fund doctrine's hold on American economics, and his Political Economy carried the argument into a standard classroom text.

works.evidence: First edition of Political Economy published by Henry Holt, New York, 1883 (American Science Series).
The Wages Question: A Treatise on Wages and the Wages Class published by Henry Holt, New York, 1876.

authors.notes: First president of the American Economic Association (1885); directed the censuses of 1870 and 1880; president of MIT 1881-1897.

authors.name: Francis Bacon
authors.bio: English lawyer and Lord Chancellor under James I, philosopher of the reform of learning. The Advancement of Learning and the Novum Organum proposed induction from organized experiment as the method of a rebuilt natural science.

works.evidence: Novum Organum published 1620 as part of the projected Instauratio Magna.
Of the Proficience and Advancement of Learning published 1605; expanded Latin version De Augmentis Scientiarum 1623.

authors.notes: Created Baron Verulam and Viscount St Alban; removed from the chancellorship for bribery in 1621.

authors.name: Francis Wrigley Hirst
authors.bio: English Liberal journalist and free-trade publicist, editor of The Economist in the Edwardian decade. His Free Trade and Other Fundamental Doctrines of the Manchester School gathered the speeches and writings of Cobden, Bright, and their followers into a single classical-liberal anthology.

works.evidence: First published London/New York 1903 (G. P. Putnam's Sons); confirmed by Amazon and Internet Archive editions.

authors.name: François Guizot
authors.bio: French historian and statesman, foreign minister and then premier under the July Monarchy. His General History of Civilization in Europe, delivered as Sorbonne lectures, gave a developmental account of European civilization that shaped Tocqueville, Mill, and Marx.

works.evidence: Histoire generale de la civilisation en Europe published 1828 from his 1828 Sorbonne lectures; Britannica and OLL concur.

authors.name: Frank H. Knight
authors.bio: American economist of the University of Chicago and a founder of its school of economics. Risk, Uncertainty and Profit drew the distinction between measurable risk and unmeasurable uncertainty and located the source of profit in the latter.

works.evidence: Published Houghton Mifflin 1921, revised from his 1916 Cornell dissertation; widely documented.

authors.name: Frank William Taussig
authors.bio: American economist of the Harvard chair and a leading authority on trade and tariff policy. The Tariff History of the United States traced the country's protective legislation across the nineteenth century and became the standard account of the subject.

works.evidence: First edition published by G. P. Putnam's Sons 1888; confirmed by Internet Archive and Amazon facsimiles.

authors.name: Franz Mehring
authors.bio: German Marxist historian and journalist, a co-founder of the Spartacus League. His historical and critical writings supplied the German socialist movement with much of its account of its own intellectual ancestry.

works.evidence: Pre-filled published_year retained; consistent with Mehring's historical writings of this period.

authors.name: Franz Oppenheimer
authors.bio: German sociologist and political economist, teacher of Ludwig Erhard. The State distinguished the economic from the political means of acquiring wealth and traced the state's origin to conquest rather than contract.

works.evidence: German original Der Staat published 1908 (written Frankfurt 1907) as part of his System der Soziologie; English translation 1922.

authors.name: Frederick Douglass
authors.bio: American abolitionist, orator, and statesman, born into slavery in Maryland and self-emancipated. The Life and Times of Frederick Douglass was the fullest of his three autobiographies, carrying his story from bondage through the Civil War into Reconstruction.

works.evidence: First published 1881; expanded edition 1892. Earliest publication of this text is 1881 per Wikipedia and DocSouth.

authors.name: Frederick Engels
authors.bio: German socialist theorist and industrialist, lifelong collaborator of Karl Marx. He co-founded historical materialism and, after Marx's death, edited the unfinished volumes of Capital into print.

works.evidence: Pre-filled; Socialisme utopique et socialisme scientifique first published 1880.
Pre-filled; Die Lage der arbeitenden Klasse in England published 1845.

authors.name: Frederick Winslow Taylor
authors.bio: American engineer who founded the movement for scientific management of industrial labour. His time-and-motion methods reorganized the factory around managerial control and provoked lasting debate over the degradation of work.

authors.name: Friedrich Nietzsche
authors.bio: German philosopher and classical philologist, briefly professor at Basel before illness ended his career. His books attacked Christian and democratic morality and advanced the will to power, eternal recurrence, and the revaluation of all values.

works.evidence: Jenseits von Gut und Boese first published 1886; standard reference.
Homer und die klassische Philologie was Nietzsche's 1869 Basel inaugural lecture, published that year.
Der Antichrist written 1888, first published 1895; standard reference.
Der Fall Wagner published 1888; Nietzsche contra Wagner compiled 1888, published 1895. Earliest component dated to 1888.
Also sprach Zarathustra Part I published 1883 (Parts I-IV 1883-1885); first publication 1883.
German original of Also sprach Zarathustra; Part I first published 1883.

authors.name: Friedrich Schiller
authors.bio: German poet, dramatist, and philosopher of history, professor at Jena and close associate of Goethe. His aesthetic and philosophical essays argued that beauty and play educate humanity toward moral and political freedom.

works.evidence: English collection of Schiller's aesthetic writings; the central piece, On the Aesthetic Education of Man, first appeared in Die Horen in 1795. Collection year approximated to its principal text.
Philosophische Briefe (Theosophie des Julius) first published 1786 in Schiller's journal Thalia.

authors.name: Friedrich von Wieser
authors.bio: Austrian economist of the early Vienna school and successor to Carl Menger. Natural Value developed the theory of imputation and gave the doctrine of opportunity cost its first systematic statement.

works.evidence: Der natuerliche Werth published Vienna 1889; English translation Natural Value 1893. Original-text year is 1889.

authors.name: G. Watts Cunningham
authors.bio: American idealist philosopher who taught at Cornell. His study of Hegel expounded the thought of the absolute idealists for an English-speaking readership.

authors.name: Gaius
authors.bio: Roman jurist of the second century AD whose biography is otherwise almost unknown. His Institutes became the standard elementary textbook of Roman law and the model for Justinian's later Institutes.

works.evidence: Institutes composed c. AD 161; ancient text with no fixed publication date, published_year left null per convention.

authors.name: Galen
authors.bio: Greek physician and philosopher of Pergamon, court doctor to Marcus Aurelius and the leading medical authority of the Roman world. De naturalibus facultatibus argued that living bodies are governed by natural faculties of attraction, retention, and expulsion, a physiology that ruled European and Islamic medicine for over a millennium.
authors.notes: Death year sometimes given as c. 200 or c. 216; modern scholarship favors c. 216 based on Arabic sources. Perseus source so published_year left null.

authors.name: Galileo Galilei
authors.bio: Italian astronomer, physicist, and mathematician of Pisa, Padua, and the Medici court at Florence. Dialogues Concerning Two New Sciences laid out the mathematics of motion and material strength, founding the modern science of mechanics.

works.evidence: Discorsi e dimostrazioni matematiche intorno a due nuove scienze published by Elzevir in Leiden, 1638 (Wikipedia, Britannica).

authors.name: Gellius, Aulus
authors.bio: Roman author and grammarian, trained in rhetoric at Rome and philosophy at Athens. The Noctes Atticae gathered miscellaneous notes on grammar, law, history, and philosophy, preserving fragments of many lost authors.
authors.notes: Birth c. 125 and death after c. 180 are conventional estimates; exact dates unknown. Perseus source so published_year left null.

authors.name: Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel
authors.bio: German philosopher of the Berlin chair, the culminating figure of German Idealism. His dialectical system traced the self-development of spirit through history and shaped nearly every current of later philosophy, Marx's above all.

authors.name: George Berkeley
authors.bio: Irish philosopher and Anglican bishop of Cloyne, the central figure of British empiricist immaterialism. His Principles and Dialogues argued that to be is to be perceived, denying the existence of mind-independent matter.

works.evidence: A Treatise Concerning the Principles of Human Knowledge first published Dublin, 1710 (standard reference).
Three Dialogues Between Hylas and Philonous first published London, 1713 (standard reference).

authors.name: George Bernard Shaw
authors.bio: Irish dramatist and critic who settled in London and became the leading pamphleteer of the Fabian Society. His economic essays argued the case for gradualist socialism against both the Marxist theory of value and laissez-faire, in the same plain combative prose as his plays.

authors.name: George Everett Partridge
authors.bio: American psychologist trained under G. Stanley Hall at Clark University, a writer on genetic and social psychology. The Psychology of Nations applied psychological theory to nationalism and the causes of war in the aftermath of the First World War.

works.evidence: The Psychology of Nations first published 1919 (HathiTrust, Internet Archive, Project Gutenberg).

authors.name: Joseph Schumpeter
authors.bio: Austrian-American economist of the Vienna school and later the Harvard faculty, trained in the Austrian marginalist tradition. works.evidence: Published in the Quarterly Journal of Economics, vol. 23 (1908-09); partial data and standard catalogs give 1908.

authors.name: Josiah Tucker
authors.bio: Welsh clergyman and economic writer, Dean of Gloucester and a pre-Smithian advocate of free trade. Four Tracts on Political and Commercial Subjects collected his arguments on commerce, naturalization, and the American colonies into one of the period's notable defenses of liberal trade policy.

works.evidence: First published 1774 by R. Raikes, Gloucester; OLL and HathiTrust catalog records confirm the year.

authors.name: Julien Offray de La Mettrie
authors.bio: French physician and materialist philosopher of the Enlightenment, driven into exile for his irreligion. His Man a Machine argued that mental life is wholly a function of the body, the boldest materialism of its age.

authors.name: Julius Caesar
authors.bio: Roman general and statesman whose campaigns and civil war ended the Republic. His two surviving commentaries narrated his Gallic campaigns and the war against Pompey in a spare third-person prose that became a model of Latin military narrative.

authors.name: Kaiten Nukariya
authors.bio: Japanese Soto Zen priest and scholar, a professor at Keio University and the Soto-shu Buddhist College in Tokyo. The Religion of the Samurai, written in English, was among the first book-length expositions of Zen Buddhism for a Western readership.

works.evidence: Published 1913 (Luzac, London); multiple reference sources date this English-language work to 1913.

authors.name: Karl Kautsky
authors.bio: Theoretician of the German Social Democracy and editor of Die Neue Zeit, the foremost Marxist authority of the Second International. His commentary on the Erfurt Programme codified orthodox Marxism, and his later quarrel with Lenin over the dictatorship of the proletariat marked the parting of social democracy from Bolshevism.

authors.name: Karl Marx
authors.bio: German philosopher, economist, and revolutionary, collaborator of Friedrich Engels and theorist of historical materialism. Capital and the shorter political writings recast political economy as a critique of capitalist production and supplied the founding texts of the socialist and communist movements.

authors.name: Knut Wicksell
authors.bio: Swedish economist of the Lund chair, founder of the Stockholm school of monetary theory. "The Influence of the Rate of Interest on Prices" set out his cumulative-process account of how a gap between the market and natural rates of interest drives the price level.

authors.name: Leon Trotsky
authors.bio: Russian revolutionary and Marxist theorist, organizer of the October insurrection and founder of the Red Army before his expulsion and exile by Stalin. His writings developed the theory of permanent revolution and a literary and political defense of the revolution against its bureaucratic turn.

authors.name: Leslie Stephen
authors.bio: English author, critic, and first editor of the Dictionary of National Biography. The English Utilitarians traced the intellectual lineage from Bentham through James and John Stuart Mill, fixing the school's standard nineteenth-century account.

works.evidence: The English Utilitarians, 3 vols., first published 1900 (Duckworth, London).

authors.name: Lewis Carroll
authors.bio: English mathematician and author, lecturer at Christ Church, Oxford, and the writer behind the Alice books. His logic works turned formal reasoning into puzzle and diagram, presenting the syllogism as a game and a system of symbolic notation.

works.evidence: Symbolic Logic, Part I, first published 1896 (Macmillan).
The Game of Logic first published 1886 (Macmillan).

authors.name: Lewis Henry Morgan
authors.bio: American lawyer and a pioneer of anthropology who studied the Iroquois and the evolution of kinship. His Ancient Society proposed a sequence of human social stages that Marx and Engels drew on for their account of the family and the state.

authors.name: Louis Auguste Blanqui
authors.bio: French revolutionary who spent half his life imprisoned for a series of insurrectionary attempts across the nineteenth century. His name became attached to the strategy of seizing power through a disciplined conspiratorial minority.

authors.name: Louis B. Boudin
authors.bio: Russian-born American labour lawyer and Marxist theorist active in the Socialist Party. His Theoretical System of Karl Marx defended the labour theory of value against its revisionist and marginalist critics.

authors.name: Lucan
authors.bio: Roman poet of the Neronian age, nephew of Seneca, forced to suicide after the Pisonian conspiracy. His unfinished epic Civil War recounted the struggle between Caesar and Pompey in a dark, rhetorical counter to Virgilian epic.

works.evidence: Perseus/ancient work; published_year left null per instructions.

authors.name: Lucian of Samosata
authors.bio: Greek-language satirist of Syrian origin, a rhetorician of the Second Sophistic who turned his training toward comic dialogue. His prose works mocked philosophers, gods, and credulity, inventing the satirical dialogue and the fantastic voyage of the True History.

authors.name: Lucretius
authors.bio: Roman poet and Epicurean. His one surviving work argues, in six books of verse, that the world is atoms and void and that understanding this frees the mind from fear.

authors.name: Lycurgus
authors.bio: Athenian orator and statesman, one of the ten Attic orators and manager of Athens' finances in the age of Demosthenes. His sole surviving speech, the prosecution of Leocrates for desertion after Chaeronea, is a patriotic indictment laced with poetic and historical quotation.

works.evidence: Perseus/ancient work; published_year left null per instructions.

authors.name: Lysander Spooner
authors.bio: American legal theorist, abolitionist, and individualist anarchist of the Massachusetts bar. His treatises argued that the Constitution authorized no slavery and ultimately bound no one, carrying natural-rights argument to anti-statist conclusions.

works.evidence: Published as a pamphlet addressed to President Cleveland in 1886.
Natural Law; or the Science of Justice published 1882.
No. VI of the No Treason series published 1870.
The Law of Intellectual Property published 1855.

authors.name: Lysias
authors.bio: Athenian metic orator and speechwriter, counted among the ten Attic canon of rhetoricians. His surviving forensic speeches set the standard for plain, character-driven prose in the Athenian courts.

authors.name: M. N. Roy
authors.bio: Indian revolutionary and theorist, founder of the Mexican and Indian communist parties and later proponent of radical humanism. His writings analyzed colonialism, the Indian national movement, and the class basis of revolution from a Marxist standpoint before his break with orthodox communism.

authors.name: Marquis de Condorcet
authors.bio: French mathematician and philosophe of the Enlightenment, associated with the Girondins during the Revolution. He defended the rights of women and the progress of reason, and his posthumous sketch of human improvement became a founding statement of the idea of progress.

works.evidence: Sur l'admission des femmes au droit de cite published in the Journal de la Societe de 1789 in July 1790.
Esquisse d'un tableau historique published posthumously in 1795.

authors.name: Martin Luther
authors.bio: German theologian and Augustinian friar whose ninety-five theses opened the Protestant Reformation. His reforming treatises and German Bible reshaped Western Christianity and the German language.

works.evidence: Collects Luther's three primary 1520 Reformation treatises; the English edition by Wace and Buchheim appeared 1883.

authors.name: Martyrium Polycarpi
authors.bio: Anonymous early Christian account, framed as a letter from the church of Smyrna recording the death of its bishop Polycarp. The text is the earliest surviving Christian martyr narrative outside the New Testament.

authors.name: Mary Mills Patrick
authors.bio: American educator and classical scholar, president of the American College for Girls at Constantinople. Her study of Sextus Empiricus introduced English readers to the philosophy of Greek Scepticism.

works.evidence: Published Cambridge, Deighton, 1899, from a 1897 Bern doctoral thesis.

authors.name: Mary Wollstonecraft
authors.bio: English writer and philosopher of the Enlightenment, an early advocate of women's rights. Her vindications of the rights of men and of women applied rational principles to politics and education and became founding texts of feminist thought.

works.evidence: A Vindication of the Rights of Men published 1790 in reply to Burke.
A Vindication of the Rights of Woman published 1792.
An Historical and Moral View of the French Revolution published 1794.

authors.name: Max Stirner
authors.bio: German post-Hegelian philosopher associated with the Young Hegelians of Berlin. The Ego and Its Own pressed egoism against state, society, and fixed ideas, and became a touchstone for individualist anarchism.

works.evidence: Der Einzige und sein Eigentum published 1844 (dated 1845).

authors.name: Max Weber
authors.bio: German sociologist, political economist, and a founder of the modern discipline of sociology. The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism traced the cultural roots of rational capitalism to ascetic Protestantism.

works.evidence: Published as essays 1904-1905 in the Archiv fur Sozialwissenschaft.

authors.name: Michel Chevalier
authors.bio: French engineer, economist, and former Saint-Simonian who became a leading advocate of free trade. His American letters reported on the industry, finance, and democracy of the United States for European readers.

works.evidence: English translation published 1839 from the French Lettres sur l'Amerique du Nord (1836).

authors.name: Michel de Montaigne
authors.bio: French nobleman, magistrate, and writer who invented the personal essay. His Essais turned skeptical self-examination into a literary method that shaped European prose.

works.evidence: Harvard Classics anthology volume 'Literary and Philosophical Essays' published 1910; Montaigne's essays themselves first appeared 1580.

authors.name: Mirza Ghalib
authors.bio: Urdu and Persian poet of the late Mughal court at Delhi, writing through the collapse of the Mughal order. His Urdu ghazals reshaped the form toward metaphysical doubt and irony and became central to the South Asian poetic canon.

works.evidence: The first edition of his Urdu Diwan was published in 1841; expanded editions followed in his lifetime.

authors.name: Moses Maimonides
authors.bio: Sephardic Jewish philosopher, jurist, and physician of Córdoba and later Fustat in Egypt, working within the Arabic Aristotelian tradition. The Guide for the Perplexed reconciled Jewish scripture with Aristotelian philosophy and became the central work of medieval Jewish thought.

works.evidence: Composed in Judeo-Arabic and completed c. 1190; date is the standard reference figure for the original composition.

authors.name: Mountifort Longfield
authors.bio: Irish economist and lawyer, the first Whately Professor of Political Economy at Trinity College Dublin. His Lectures advanced an early theory of demand intensity and marginal value that anticipated the later marginalist economics.

works.evidence: Lectures delivered in Trinity term 1833 and published by Milliken in Dublin in 1834.

authors.name: Nassau William Senior
authors.bio: English classical economist and lawyer, the first Drummond Professor of Political Economy at Oxford and an adviser on the New Poor Law. His writings worked to give classical economics a more deductive, scientific footing and introduced the abstinence theory of capital.

works.evidence: Four Introductory Lectures on Political Economy published by Longmans in 1852.

authors.name: Niccolò Machiavelli
authors.bio: Florentine diplomat, political theorist, and secretary of the Republic, sidelined after the Medici restoration. His writings founded a realist tradition of political analysis that examined power as it operates rather than as it ought to be.

works.evidence: Dell'arte della guerra published in Florence in 1521, the only major work printed in his lifetime.
Il Principe written 1513 but first printed posthumously in 1532.

authors.name: Nicholas Barbon
authors.bio: English physician, builder, and economic writer active in the rebuilding of London after the Great Fire and a pioneer of fire insurance. A Discourse of Trade set out an early case for the value of money as conventional and for consumption as the engine of trade.

works.evidence: A Discourse of Trade first published in London in 1690.

authors.name: Nikolai Bukharin
authors.bio: Bolshevik economist and editor of Pravda, the party's leading theorist in the years after Lenin. His ABC of Communism and Historical Materialism were the standard expositions of Bolshevik doctrine until he was tried and shot in the Great Purge.

authors.name: Nikolai Bukharin and Evgeni Preobrazhensky
authors.bio: The Bolshevik theorists Nikolai Bukharin and Evgeni Preobrazhensky, writing in the first years of Soviet power. Their ABC of Communism became the most widely read popular exposition of the party programme.

authors.name: Old Testament
authors.bio: Anonymous and composite collection of Hebrew scriptures assembled over centuries by many hands and editors. The texts became the shared canon of Judaism and the first part of the Christian Bible.
authors.notes: Composite work of many anonymous authors and redactors over centuries; no single author and no birth/death dates. Perseus source, so published_year left null per instructions.

authors.name: Oscar Wilde
authors.bio: Irish playwright, novelist, and critic, a leading figure of the Aesthetic movement in late-Victorian London. The Soul of Man under Socialism argued for socialism as the condition for individual self-realization and the freedom of the artist.

works.evidence: Provided data gives 1891, matching first publication in the Fortnightly Review.

authors.name: Otto Bauer
authors.bio: Austrian Marxist theorist and Social Democratic politician, a leading figure of Austromarxism and the Austrian republic's early foreign minister. His writings developed Marxist analyses of nationality, reformism, and the contradictions of postwar capitalism.

authors.name: Otto Rühle
authors.bio: German council communist and educator, a Reichstag deputy who broke with the Social Democrats to oppose the First World War. His biography of Marx presented Marx's life and thought for a working-class readership from a council-communist standpoint.

works.evidence: Provided data gives 1928, matching the German original Karl Marx: Leben und Werk.

authors.name: Ovid
authors.bio: Roman poet of the Augustan age, exiled by Augustus to the Black Sea coast. His verse on love, myth, and transformation, above all the Metamorphoses, became a primary channel of classical mythology to later European literature.
