authors.name: Pierre-Joseph Proudhon
authors.bio: French printer and self-taught economist, the first man to call himself an anarchist. His declaration that property is theft and his schemes for mutualist credit founded the anarchist tradition and drew Marx's polemical fire.

authors.name: Pieter de la Court
authors.bio: Dutch cloth merchant and republican economist of Leiden, allied with the regime of Johan de Witt. His True Interest and Political Maxims argued the commercial case for free trade and against monarchy in the Dutch Republic.

authors.name: Pindar
authors.bio: Theban lyric poet of the Greek archaic age, the foremost composer of choral victory odes. His epinicia for athletes at the Olympic, Pythian, Nemean, and Isthmian games survive as the fullest body of Greek choral lyric.

authors.name: Plato
authors.bio: Athenian philosopher, student of Socrates and teacher of Aristotle. His dialogues made philosophy a written art and set its agenda for the next two thousand years.

authors.name: Plautus, Titus Maccius
authors.bio: Roman comic playwright of the early Republic, adapting Greek New Comedy for the Latin stage. His twenty surviving fabulae palliatae are the earliest complete works of Latin literature and shaped later European comedy.

authors.name: Pliny, the Elder
authors.bio: Roman equestrian official, naturalist, and naval commander who died observing the eruption of Vesuvius. His Naturalis Historia gathered the knowledge of the ancient world into the first comprehensive encyclopedia.

authors.name: Plutarch
authors.bio: Greek biographer, essayist, and priest at Delphi under the Roman Empire. His Parallel Lives paired Greek and Roman figures while the Moralia collected his essays on ethics, religion, and philosophy.

authors.name: Polybius
authors.bio: Greek statesman of the Achaean League taken as a hostage to Rome, where he turned historian. His Histories explained Rome's rise to Mediterranean dominance and advanced a pragmatic, cause-seeking method of historiography.

authors.name: Polycarp
authors.bio: Bishop of Smyrna and one of the Apostolic Fathers, traditionally a disciple of John the Evangelist, who died a martyr. His Epistle to the Philippians is a key witness to early Christian doctrine and to the formation of the New Testament canon.

authors.name: Pseudo-Caesar
authors.bio: Conventional label for the anonymous Roman authors who continued Caesar's war commentaries. The De Bello Africo and De Bello Alexandrino narrate campaigns of the civil war and were transmitted within the Caesarian corpus though not written by Caesar.

authors.name: Pseudo-Justinus Martyr
authors.bio: Conventional label for the anonymous author of works transmitted under the name of Justin Martyr but not his. The Epistle to Diognetus is an early Christian apologetic letter of uncertain date and authorship defending the faith to a pagan inquirer.

authors.name: Pseudo-Lucian
authors.bio: Conventional label for the anonymous authors of works transmitted in the Lucianic corpus but judged not to be by Lucian of Samosata. These pieces imitate his satirical and rhetorical manner and circulated under his name in antiquity.

authors.name: Pseudo-Plutarch
authors.bio: Conventional label for the anonymous authors of works transmitted in the Plutarchan corpus but not written by Plutarch. The pieces include doxographical and antiquarian compilations that circulated under his name within the Moralia.

authors.name: Quintilian
authors.bio: Roman rhetorician from Hispania and the first holder of a state-funded chair of rhetoric at Rome. His Institutio Oratoria laid out a complete program for educating the orator and became a touchstone of rhetorical theory.

authors.name: Quintus Tullius Cicero
authors.bio: Roman senator, soldier, and provincial governor, the younger brother of Marcus Tullius Cicero. The Commentariolum Petitionis attributed to him offered tactical advice on running for the consulship and survives as a handbook of Roman electioneering.

authors.name: Ralph Barton Perry
authors.bio: American philosopher of the Harvard chair and a leader of the New Realist movement, student of William James. The Approach to Philosophy laid out philosophy as a practical engagement with experience and his later thought codified the realist reaction against idealism.

works.evidence: First published by C. Scribner's Sons, New York, 1905; preface dated Cambridge, March 1905 (Gutenberg, Internet Archive).

authors.name: Rebecca Cooper
authors.bio: American philosopher who wrote her doctoral study on the relation between Hegelian and Marxian logic. The Logical Influence of Hegel on Marx traced the dialectical method from Hegel's system into Marx's economic and historical argument.

authors.name: René Descartes
authors.bio: French philosopher and mathematician, founder of modern rationalism and inventor of analytic geometry. His Discourse and Meditations made systematic doubt the starting point of philosophy and set the mind-body problem at the center of modern thought.

works.evidence: Discours de la methode first published anonymously at Leiden, 1637.

authors.name: Richard Falckenberg

authors.name: Richard Overton
authors.bio: English pamphleteer and a leading writer of the Leveller movement during the Civil War. An Arrow Against All Tyrants argued from natural individual self-propriety to inalienable rights against parliamentary and aristocratic power.

works.evidence: Published 12 October 1646 from Newgate prison (OLL Leveller Tracts).

authors.name: Richard Price
authors.bio: Welsh dissenting minister, moral philosopher, and writer on probability and public finance. Observations on the Nature of Civil Liberty defended the American colonists' cause and circulated widely on both sides of the Atlantic.

works.evidence: First published London, T. Cadell, February 1776 (OLL, Internet Archive).

authors.name: Richard T. Ely
authors.bio: American economist trained in the German historical school and a founder of the American Economic Association. The work circulated under his name supplied an introduction and editorial framing to a standard history of political economy used in American economics teaching.

works.evidence: A History of Political Economy was written by John Kells Ingram (1888); Ely's role was introduction/editor of the enlarged 1915 edition (OLL attributes the title to Ely).

authors.name: Richard Whately
authors.bio: English logician, Drummond Professor of Political Economy at Oxford, and later Archbishop of Dublin. His Introductory Lectures argued for political economy as a neutral science distinct from moral exhortation.

works.evidence: First published London, B. Fellowes, 1831, from lectures delivered Easter term 1831 (OLL, Internet Archive).

authors.name: Richard William Church
authors.bio: English clergyman, Dean of St Paul's, and historian associated with the Oxford Movement. His Bacon for the English Men of Letters series gave a compact critical account of Francis Bacon's life and thought.

works.evidence: Bacon (English Men of Letters series) first published by Macmillan, 1884.

authors.name: Robert Franklin Hoxie
authors.bio: American labor economist at the University of Chicago and an early student of trade unionism as a social phenomenon. Trade Unionism in the United States, assembled from his papers after his death, set out a functional typology of American unions.

works.evidence: Published posthumously by D. Appleton, 1917, edited from his notes (Wikipedia, Internet Archive).

authors.name: Robert Owen
authors.bio: Welsh manufacturer at New Lanark and a founder of the cooperative and utopian socialist tradition. A New View of Society argued that character is formed by environment and proposed reform of factory conditions and education to remake it.

works.evidence: Existing record year retained; first complete edition 1816 (essays 1813-1816).

authors.name: Rosa Luxemburg
authors.bio: Polish-born theorist and agitator of the German and Polish socialist movements, co-founder of the Spartacus League. Her work on capital accumulation, the mass strike and revolutionary democracy made her the foremost Marxist critic of both reformism and Bolshevik centralism.

authors.name: Roscoe Pound
authors.bio: American jurist, Dean of Harvard Law School, and the leading exponent of sociological jurisprudence. An Introduction to the Philosophy of Law set out his program for law understood through its social ends rather than abstract logic.

works.evidence: An Introduction to the Philosophy of Law (Storrs Lectures) first published by Yale University Press, 1922.

authors.name: Rudolf Hilferding
authors.bio: Austrian-German Marxist economist and twice finance minister of the Weimar Republic. His Finance Capital analyzed the fusion of banking and industry into monopoly and supplied a foundation for later theories of imperialism.

authors.name: Sallust
authors.bio: Roman politician and historian of the late Republic, a partisan of Caesar who retired to write after his political career. authors.name: Samuel Smiles

authors.bio: 19th-century Urdu poet and court poet of the last Mughal emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar. Known for his classical ghazals and mastery of traditional Urdu poetic forms.

authors.name: Simon Dubnow
authors.bio: Russian-Jewish historian and theorist of Jewish national autonomism, murdered in the Riga ghetto. His essay on the philosophy of Jewish history argued for the secular continuity of the Jewish people through its communal institutions rather than its religion or state.

works.evidence: English translation first published 1903 by the Jewish Publication Society; original Russian essay 1893

authors.name: Simon Newcomb
authors.bio: Canadian-born American astronomer and mathematician who also wrote on economics and political economy. The A B C of Finance explained money and labor questions to a popular audience in defense of hard-money orthodoxy.

works.evidence: First published 1877 (OLL, University of Michigan Making of America)

authors.name: Simonde de Sismondi
authors.bio: Genevan historian and economist whose later work broke with Smithian optimism. His writings on political economy advanced the first systematic account of overproduction and underconsumption crises, anticipating later critiques of laissez-faire.

works.evidence: Provided published_year 1815 retained; corresponds to his 'Political Economy' article for the Edinburgh Encyclopaedia

authors.name: Sir Dudley North
authors.bio: English merchant in the Levant trade and Tory financial official who wrote on commerce in his retirement. Discourses upon Trade made an early free-trade argument against mercantilist restrictions and the regulation of interest rates.

works.evidence: Published anonymously in 1691, the year of North's death

authors.name: Sir Frederick Pollock
authors.bio: English jurist, legal historian, and longtime correspondent of Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr. His treatise on torts and his lectures on the common law systematized English private law around its underlying principles and traced its distinctive character.

works.evidence: Carpentier Lectures delivered and published at Columbia University Press, 1912
First edition of the treatise published 1887

authors.name: Sir Robert Filmer
authors.bio: English royalist political theorist whose defense of absolute monarchy was published only after his death. Patriarcha grounded kingly authority in the paternal power of Adam and became the foil that Locke wrote his First Treatise to demolish.

works.evidence: Written before 1653 but first published posthumously in 1680

authors.name: Sophocles
authors.bio: Athenian tragedian of the fifth century and one of the three whose plays survive, a contemporary of Pericles. His seven extant tragedies, including Antigone and the Oedipus plays, reshaped the form by adding a third actor and remain central to the Western dramatic canon.

authors.name: St. George William Joseph Stock
authors.bio: English classical scholar and logician at Oxford who wrote textbooks and primers on philosophy. His Deductive Logic served generations as a teaching manual and A Guide to Stoicism introduced the school's ethics to general readers.

authors.name: Strabo
authors.bio: Greek geographer and historian from Amasia in Pontus, writing under Augustus and Tiberius. The Geography compiled the known world into seventeen books and became the principal ancient survey of lands, peoples, and the discipline itself.
authors.notes: Dates are conventional (c. 64 BC to c. AD 24); some references give the death as late as AD 23 or 24. Perseus work: published_year null.

authors.name: Suetonius
authors.bio: Roman biographer and imperial secretary under Hadrian, drawing on archival access to the emperors' lives. The Lives of the Twelve Caesars set the template for political biography, ordering each reign by anecdote, character, and administrative record.

works.evidence: Composed c. AD 121 under Hadrian; ancient text, no fixed publication year, so left null.

authors.notes: Birth and death conventional (c. AD 69 to after AD 122). The individual Caesar lives are Perseus sources; the oll Lives of the Twelve Caesars is the same ancient text, dated null as antique.

authors.name: Surendranath Dasgupta
authors.bio: Bengali philosopher and Sanskrit scholar, professor at Presidency College and the University of Calcutta. His multi-volume A History of Indian Philosophy gave Western and Indian readers a systematic, text-based account of the classical schools.

works.evidence: Volume 1 first published by Cambridge University Press in 1922.

authors.name: Tacitus, Cornelius
authors.bio: Roman senator, orator, and historian of the early Empire under Trajan. The Annals and Histories traced the Julio-Claudian and Flavian principate with a compressed, moralizing prose that shaped the Western idea of historical writing.
authors.notes: Dates conventional (c. AD 56 to c. AD 120). All works Perseus sources: published_year null.

authors.name: Terence
authors.bio: Roman comic playwright of North African origin, freedman in the circle of Scipio Aemilianus. His six surviving comedies adapted Greek New Comedy into a refined Latin that became a schoolroom model of style for centuries.
authors.notes: Birth conventionally c. 195 or 185 BC; death c. 159 BC. All works Perseus sources: published_year null.

authors.name: The Levellers
authors.bio: English radical movement of the Civil War period, organized around John Lilburne, Richard Overton, and William Walwyn in the New Model Army and London. Their pamphlets and the Putney debates pressed for popular sovereignty, religious toleration, and an extended franchise.

works.evidence: The Army (Putney) debates took place 1647-49; the recorded transcripts were published posthumously (Clarke Papers, 1891; A.S.P. Woodhouse's Puritanism and Liberty edition, 1938), so no single original publication year applies.

authors.notes: A movement rather than an individual, so birth/death null; floruit c. 1645-1660.

authors.name: The Venerable Bede
authors.bio: Northumbrian monk and scholar of the monastery at Wearmouth-Jarrow. The Ecclesiastical History of the English People organized the Anglo-Saxon past into a continuous Christian narrative and fixed the Anno Domini dating system in Western use.

works.evidence: Historia ecclesiastica gentis Anglorum completed c. AD 731.

authors.notes: Birth conventionally c. AD 672 or 673.

authors.name: Theodore Dwight Woolsey
authors.bio: American classicist and political theorist, president of Yale College and writer on international law. He edited and enlarged Francis Lieber's On Civil Liberty and Self-Government, extending its argument on institutional liberty for a postbellum readership.

works.evidence: The text is Francis Lieber's treatise (first ed. 1853); the Woolsey-edited revised and enlarged edition was published 1877 by Lippincott.

authors.notes: The underlying work was authored by Francis Lieber; Woolsey is the editor of the enlarged edition catalogued under his name here.

authors.name: Thomas Clarkson
authors.bio: English abolitionist and campaigner, co-founder of the Society for the Abolition of the Slave Trade. His prize-winning Essay on the Slavery and Commerce of the Human Species assembled the evidentiary case that drove the British abolition movement.

works.evidence: First published 1786 (expanded from his 1785 Latin Cambridge prize essay).

authors.name: Thomas Gordon
authors.bio: Scottish writer and Commonwealthman, co-author with John Trenchard of Cato's Letters. A Discourse of Standing Armies argued the country-Whig case against a permanent peacetime military as a threat to civil liberty.

works.evidence: An Argument/Discourse of Standing Armies published 1722.

authors.notes: Birth year is uncertain (commonly given as c. 1691); some sources leave it unknown.

authors.name: Thomas Hobbes
authors.bio: English philosopher of Malmesbury, tutor and secretary in the Cavendish household and theorist of sovereignty. Leviathan derived absolute political authority from a covenant among self-interested individuals and founded modern social-contract thought.

works.evidence: Leviathan first published in English in 1651.

authors.name: Thomas Hodgskin
authors.bio: English naval officer turned political economist and journalist, lecturer at the London Mechanics' Institution. His writings argued that labor is the true source of value and that property rights rest on nature rather than legal privilege.

works.evidence: Lecture delivered and published 1843 (White Conduit House, Islington).
The Natural and Artificial Right of Property Contrasted published 1832 (lectures of 1829).

authors.name: Thomas More
authors.bio: English humanist, lawyer, and Lord Chancellor under Henry VIII, executed for refusing the royal supremacy. Utopia coined the word and gave European political thought its enduring model of the imagined commonwealth used to criticize the existing one.

works.evidence: Utopia first printed in Latin at Leuven, 1516; standard reference date.

authors.name: Thomas Paine
authors.bio: English-born corset-maker turned American and French revolutionary pamphleteer. Common Sense argued for American independence in plain language and sold in unprecedented numbers, and Rights of Man defended the French Revolution against Burke.

works.evidence: Rights of Man Part I published 1791 (Part II 1792); first-publication year is 1791.

authors.name: Thomas Reid and others
authors.bio: Scottish philosopher of the Aberdeen and Glasgow chairs and founder of the common-sense school, here heading an anthology of that tradition. The Scottish philosophy of common sense answered Humean skepticism by treating the deliverances of ordinary perception and judgment as first principles.

works.evidence: G. A. Johnston's anthology Selections from the Scottish Philosophy of Common Sense first published 1915 (Open Court); the texts excerpted are 18th-19th century.

authors.notes: Dates given are Thomas Reid's (1710-1796), the lead figure; the volume is a 20th-century anthology of multiple Scottish authors. Nationality Scottish reflects the school.

authors.name: Thomas Robert Malthus
authors.bio: English clergyman and political economist, the first professor of political economy in Britain, at the East India Company college at Haileybury. An Essay on the Principle of Population argued that population tends to outrun subsistence and reshaped debate over poverty, wages, and reform.

works.evidence: First edition published anonymously 1798; date is in the title and standard reference.
Definitions in Political Economy first published 1827.
Principles of Political Economy first published 1820 (2nd ed. posthumous 1836).

authors.name: Thomas Taylor
authors.bio: English Neoplatonist and translator known as the Platonist, the first to render the complete works of Plato and Aristotle into English. His translations and commentaries carried Plato, Proclus, and Iamblichus to the Romantic poets, transcendentalists, and later esoteric readers.

works.evidence: Introduction prefacing Taylor's complete Works of Plato, published 1804.

authors.notes: Dates confirmed via Wikipedia: born 15 May 1758, died 1 November 1835.

authors.name: Thorstein Veblen
authors.bio: American economist and sociologist of Norwegian immigrant background, founder of the institutionalist school. The Theory of the Leisure Class introduced conspicuous consumption and analyzed status display as the driver of economic behavior in industrial society.

works.evidence: The Theory of the Leisure Class first published 1899; standard reference date.

authors.name: Thucydides
authors.bio: Athenian general and historian of the war between Athens and Sparta, which he fought in, was exiled from, and recorded with a rigor that made his book the model of critical history.

authors.name: Tibullus
authors.bio: Roman elegiac poet of the circle of Messalla, ranked with Propertius among the major Augustan love elegists. His two books of elegies, transmitted with the Corpus Tibullianum, gave Latin love poetry its smooth, idealized rural manner.

works.evidence: Perseus / ancient source; no modern publication year assigned.

authors.notes: Birth c. 55 BC and death 19 BC are conventional but approximate. The Sulpicia elegies are part of the Corpus Tibullianum but attributed to Sulpicia rather than Tibullus himself.

authors.name: Titus Livius (Livy)
authors.bio: Roman historian from Patavium (Padua), author of the great Augustan-era history of Rome. Ab urbe condita narrated Rome from its founding through to his own day and became the canonical literary account of the Republic.
authors.notes: Birth 59 BC and death AD 17 are the standard dates (some sources give 64 BC / AD 12).

authors.name: Unknown
authors.bio: Anonymous or collectively transmitted authorship spanning the Sanskrit Dharmaśāstra (smṛti) tradition, Old Javanese tutur and kakawin literature, and Old English elegiac verse. These texts carry inherited law, ritual, cosmology, and lament shaped over generations rather than by a single named author.

authors.name: Vatsyayana
authors.bio: Indian author traditionally credited with compiling the foundational Sanskrit treatise on erotics, working from earlier kama literature. The Kama Sutra systematized the science of desire, courtship, and household life within the framework of the classical aims of human life.

works.evidence: Ancient Sanskrit text, c. 3rd century CE; no fixed publication year. Burton/Arbuthnot English translation 1883.

authors.notes: Flourished c. 3rd century CE; exact dates unknown, so birth/death null per instructions. Nationality given as Indian (ancient India).

authors.name: Victor Cousin
authors.bio: French philosopher and educational administrator, founder of the eclectic or spiritualist school and reformer of the national university system. Du vrai, du beau et du bien argued that philosophy should select what is true across rival systems and grounded a doctrine of the true, the beautiful, and the good.

works.evidence: Translation of Du vrai, du beau et du bien, first published in book form 1836 (from 1818 lectures); English editions 1853-54.

authors.notes: Dates confirmed (1792-1867). Original French work 1836; using first-publication year of the text.

authors.name: Virgil
authors.bio: Rome's national poet. The Aeneid, commissioned under Augustus and unfinished at his death, gave Rome its founding epic and Europe its model of literary epic for centuries.

authors.name: Vitruvius Pollio
authors.bio: Roman architect and military engineer of the age of Augustus, to whom his treatise is dedicated. De architectura is the only surviving classical work on architecture and transmitted the principles of building, proportion, and engineering to the Renaissance and after.

works.evidence: Perseus / ancient source; De architectura composed c. 30-15 BCE, no modern publication year.

authors.notes: Birth c. 80 BC and death c. 15 BC are conventional estimates; biographical dates are uncertain.

authors.name: Vladimir Lenin
authors.bio: Russian revolutionary and Marxist theorist, founder of the Bolshevik party and the Soviet state. His writings turned Marxism into a doctrine of the vanguard party and seizure of power, and governed communist movements for the rest of the century.
authors.notes: Standard reference dates and nationality. 'Philosophical Notebooks' is a posthumous compilation of his 1914-16 reading notes, first published in the late 1920s as Collected Works vol. 38.

works.evidence: Given as 1919; matches written date of the essay.
Given as 1916; standard date of first publication.

authors.name: Voltaire
authors.bio: French Enlightenment writer, satirist, and pamphleteer, born Francois-Marie Arouet and the most public intellectual of his age. His campaigns against intolerance and clerical authority made literary celebrity a force in public argument.
authors.notes: Dates and nationality standard. The OLL 'Toleration and Other Essays' is the English collection edited and translated by Joseph McCabe, published by Putnam in 1912.

works.evidence: Joseph McCabe's English translation collection, G. P. Putnam's Sons, 1912.

authors.name: W. Tudor Jones
authors.bio: Welsh Unitarian minister and philosopher, the leading English-language exponent of Rudolf Eucken's spiritual idealism. His expository books carried Eucken's anti-materialist philosophy of life to a British and American readership.
authors.notes: Dictionary of Welsh Biography confirms 1865-1946, born Pontrhydfendigaid, Cardiganshire; Unitarian minister and philosopher who studied under Eucken at Jena.

works.evidence: First edition dated 1912 (AbeBooks/MW Books, Williams & Norgate).

authors.name: Walter Bagehot
authors.bio: English banker, essayist, and editor of The Economist, writing on constitutional and monetary questions. Lombard Street explained how the Bank of England should act as lender of last resort, and became the founding text of central-banking practice.
authors.notes: Lombard Street first published 1873.

works.evidence: Lombard Street first published by Henry S. King & Co., London, 1873.

authors.name: Wilhelm von Humboldt
authors.bio: Prussian statesman, linguist, and philosopher of education, founder of the University of Berlin. The Sphere and Duties of Government argued that the state should confine itself to security, a limited-government classic that shaped John Stuart Mill.
authors.notes: The essay 'Ideen zu einem Versuch, die Grenzen der Wirksamkeit des Staats zu bestimmen' was written in 1792 but suppressed; first published in full in German in 1851, and the English translation (Coulthard) appeared 1854. Original publication of the text = 1851.

works.evidence: Written 1792, first published posthumously in German in 1851; the OLL English title 'The Sphere and Duties of Government' is Coulthard's 1854 translation of that text.

authors.name: William Allan Chapple
authors.bio: New Zealand physician and politician who also sat in the British House of Commons, and an advocate of eugenic policy. The Fertility of the Unfit pressed the case for curbing reproduction among those it deemed degenerate, an early statement of antipodean eugenics.
authors.notes: Born 1864, died 1936; physician, NZ House of Representatives then UK House of Commons (Stirlingshire, Dumfriesshire). 'The Fertility of the Unfit' published 1903.

works.evidence: Whitcombe & Tombs / Longmans, 1903; multiple editions and Amazon listing confirm '1903'.

authors.name: William Brough
authors.bio: Scottish-born American businessman and monetary writer, a pioneer of the early petroleum industry turned amateur economist. The Natural Law of Money defended a metallic, privately governed currency and gave one of the period's clearest accounts of Gresham's Law.
authors.notes: Born 1826 in Kelso, Scotland; emigrated as a child and spent his career in the United States, conventionally classed as an American economic writer. 'The Natural Law of Money' published 1894 by Putnam.

works.evidence: G. P. Putnam's Sons, 1894 (Internet Archive / Econlib).

authors.name: William Godwin
authors.bio: English political philosopher and novelist, a founder of philosophical anarchism and husband of Mary Wollstonecraft. Of Population was his late reply to Malthus, disputing the inevitability of population pressure on subsistence.
authors.notes: Of Population: An Enquiry Concerning the Power of Increase in the Numbers of Mankind, published 1820 as Godwin's answer to Malthus.

authors.name: William Graham Sumner
authors.bio: American sociologist and political economist of the Yale chair, a leading classical liberal and Social Darwinist. His essays and lectures defended free trade, the gold standard, and the self-supporting 'Forgotten Man' against state redistribution.
authors.notes: Several titles are posthumous Yale University Press collections edited by Albert Galloway Keller.

works.evidence: Posthumous collection, Yale University Press, 1913, ed. A. G. Keller.
Posthumous collection, Yale University Press, 1918, ed. A. G. Keller (title lecture orig. 1883).
Posthumous collection, Yale University Press, 1911, ed. A. G. Keller.

authors.name: William James
authors.bio: American philosopher and psychologist at Harvard, a founder of pragmatism and of psychology as a laboratory discipline. His later lectures and essays developed a pluralistic metaphysics and the doctrine of radical empiricism.
authors.notes: Dates and nationality standard. 'Essays in Radical Empiricism' is posthumous, edited by R. B. Perry, 1912.

works.evidence: Longmans, Green & Co., 1909; based on the 1908 Hibbert Lectures.
Posthumous collection ed. R. B. Perry, Longmans, Green & Co., 1912.

authors.name: William Minto
authors.bio: Scottish critic, journalist, and Regius Professor of Logic and English Literature at Aberdeen. His Logic, Inductive and Deductive distilled the inductive tradition of Bain and Mill into a teaching textbook.
authors.notes: Born 1845, died March 1893 in Aberdeen; 'Logic, Inductive and Deductive' published 1893, effectively his last work.

works.evidence: John Murray, London, 1893 (Internet Archive / Gutenberg title page).

authors.name: William Molyneux
authors.bio: Irish natural philosopher and politician, friend of John Locke and founder of the Dublin Philosophical Society. The Case of Ireland argued that the English Parliament had no right to legislate for Ireland, a foundational text of Irish constitutional nationalism.
authors.notes: The Case of Ireland's Being Bound by Acts of Parliament in England, Stated, published 1698, the year of his death.

works.evidence: First published Dublin, 1698 (year of Molyneux's death).

authors.name: William Morris
authors.bio: English poet, designer, and craftsman who turned from the Pre-Raphaelite circle to revolutionary socialism. His lectures and the utopian romance News from Nowhere fused aesthetic critique with a vision of work and society remade for pleasure rather than profit.

authors.name: William Morris and E. Belfort Bax
authors.bio: The English socialists William Morris and Ernest Belfort Bax, collaborators in the Socialist League. Together they wrote Socialism: Its Growth and Outcome, a history and exposition of the socialist case.

authors.name: William Sharp McKechnie
authors.bio: Scottish legal scholar of the University of Glasgow, lecturer in constitutional law and history and later professor of conveyancing. His detailed clause-by-clause Magna Carta commentary became the standard scholarly treatment of the Great Charter of King John.

works.evidence: First edition published Glasgow: Maclehose, 1905; revised second edition 1914.

authors.notes: Born Paisley 1863, died 1930 (Wikipedia/Internet Archive). First edition of Magna Carta commentary is 1905; a substantially revised edition appeared 1914.

authors.name: William Stanley Jevons
authors.bio: English economist and logician of Owens College and University College London, a founder of marginal utility theory. The Theory of Political Economy recast value on the basis of marginal utility and helped open the neoclassical turn in economics.

works.evidence: Given as 1866 in source data; paper read to the British Association in 1862, published 1866.

authors.name: William Stebbing
authors.bio: English barrister, journalist, and editor associated with The Times and All Souls College, Oxford. His Analysis of Mr. Mill's System of Logic condensed John Stuart Mill's treatise into a student abstract that long served as a study guide.

works.evidence: First published London: Longmans, Green, 1864 (AbeBooks first-edition listing; Rooke Books).

authors.notes: Dates 1832-1926 from provided data and Wikipedia. Work first published 1864.

authors.name: Wordsworth Donisthorpe
authors.bio: English barrister, individualist anarchist, and cinematography pioneer active in the Liberty and Property Defence League. His treatises Individualism and Law in a Free State worked out a politics grounded in equal liberty and minimal state coercion.

works.evidence: Individualism: A System of Politics first published Macmillan, London, 1889.
Law in a Free State first published Macmillan, 1895.

authors.name: Xenophon
authors.bio: Athenian soldier, historian, and follower of Socrates who led the Greek mercenaries of the Anabasis out of Persia. His Hellenica, Socratic writings, and treatises on practical life preserve much of fourth-century Greek history and the memory of Socrates.
authors.notes: Birth c. 430 BC, death c. 354 BC are conventional approximations. Perseus works left with null published_year per ancient-text rule.

authors.name: Yves Guyot
authors.bio: French economist, journalist, and politician of the classical-liberal school, a deputy and minister of public works. His polemics against collectivism argued that state ownership and socialist schemes fail on both economic and moral grounds.

works.evidence: English translation Socialistic Fallacies published 1910 (Internet Archive copy dated 1910).
The Tyranny of Socialism (trans. J. H. Levy) published 1894.
English edition (trans. H. F. Baker, Macmillan) published 1914.
